payload.name: stylohyoid-ligament
payload.scope: People made the stylohyoid ligament construct to map the band suspending the hyoid bone from the styloid process of the skull, so that anatomists and skull-base surgeons can orient the hyoid suspensions and diagnose its calcifications causing Eagle syndrome.

definition.body: The stylohyoid ligament is a human-authored anatomical construct mapping the band of fibrous tissue connecting the styloid process of the temporal bone to the greater horn of the hyoid bone, suspending the hyoid from the skull base. Parameters: (1) the attachments - the styloid process of the temporal bone superiorly, the greater horn of the hyoid bone inferiorly; (2) the structure - a flat fibrous band approximately 3 cm long through which the stylohyoid muscle passes, the ligament remaining behind it; (3) the function - transmitting force between the skull base and the hyoid and limiting hyoid excursion during swallowing and mastication; (4) the clinical significance - calcification and elongation of the ligament and styloid process producing the pain of Eagle syndrome. It persists as a standard anatomical structure in human anatomy texts, skull-base surgical references, and radiology. e.g.: the stylohyoid ligament depicted in the skull chapter of Moore Clinically Orientated Anatomy, 9th edition; stylohyoid ligament calcification on lateral skull radiograph in Eagle syndrome in a radiology teaching file; the stylohyoid ligament preserved in a parotidectomy approach in a head and neck surgery atlas | not: the stylohyoid muscle (the muscle passing through the ligament, a distinct structure); the styloid process (the bone to which the ligament attaches); the temporomandibular joint (the mandibular articulation, a different relation) [formal: ligamentum stylohyoideum | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: paraglottic-space
payload.scope: People made the paraglottic space construct to map the fat-filled lateral compartment of the larynx, so that radiologists and head and neck surgeons can assess tumor spread in laryngeal cancer staging and plan surgical approaches.

definition.body: The paraglottic space is a human-authored anatomical construct mapping the potential fat-filled compartment on each side of the larynx, bounded medially by the perichondrium of the thyroid lamina and laterally by the thyrohyoid membrane, extending from the hyoid to the cricoid, that provides the plane of tumor spread in laryngeal carcinoma. Parameters: (1) the boundaries - medially the perichondrium of the thyroid lamina, laterally the thyrohyoid membrane inferiorly blending into the cricothyroid membrane, superiorly at the level of the hyoid, inferiorly at the cricoid; (2) the contents - fat and loose connective tissue with lymphatic channels, carrying the recurrent laryngeal nerve and the inferior laryngeal vessels in its lateral part; (3) the relations - the lateral continuation of the pre-epiglottic space, the two together enclosing the larynx; (4) the clinical significance - the plane of spread of T2 laryngeal carcinoma, with invasion of the space, loss of the fat plane on CT or MRI, marking T3 staging. It persists as a maintained anatomical landmark in head and neck radiology, laryngeal cancer staging, and surgical planning. e.g.: the paraglottic space evaluated on axial CT in AJCC staging of laryngeal carcinoma; paraglottic fat plane loss on MRI marking extralaryngeal extension of a T3 glottic cancer; the paraglottic space opened during a hemilaryngofissure approach in a head and neck surgery atlas | not: the pre-epiglottic space (the anterior compartment bounded by the thyroepiglottic ligament, a distinct compartment); the paralaryngeal space (the lateral neck space outside the larynx, including the strap muscles); the paraglottic perichondrium (the medial boundary, not the space) [formal: spatium paraglotticum | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: laryngocele
payload.scope: People made the laryngocele construct to map the cystic distension of the laryngeal saccule, so that otolaryngologists and head and neck surgeons can diagnose and excise the internal and external neck masses it produces.

definition.body: The laryngocele is a human-authored anatomical construct mapping the mucosa-lined cystic distension of the laryngeal saccule, filled with air or mucus, of the internal kind remaining within the larynx and the external kind extending through the thyrohyoid membrane into the neck. Parameters: (1) the origin - distension of the laryngeal saccule, the blind pouch of the anterior laryngeal ventricle; (2) the types - internal, confined within the larynx and distending the ventricular area, external, protruding through the thyrohyoid membrane, and combined; (3) the contents - air in a congenital laryngocele that still communicates with the ventricle, mucus in an acquired laryngocele whose neck is occluded; (4) the clinical significance - a neck mass fluctuating with straining or Valsalva, airway obstruction or hoarseness, treated by excision of the saccule. It persists as a standard diagnostic and surgical entity in otolaryngology, head and neck surgery, and radiology. e.g.: an external laryngocele as a neck mass fluctuating with Valsalva on CT in Cummings Otolaryngology, 6th edition; an internal laryngocele visualized on flexible laryngoscopy in Bailey's Head and Neck Otolaryngology; transoral excision of a laryngocele with saccule removal in a Laryngoscope case report | not: a thyroglossal duct cyst (midline embryological remnant, different origin); the laryngeal saccule (the normal blind pouch that the laryngocele distends); a pre-epiglottic abscess (an infection, not a saccule distension) [formal: laryngocele | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.note: The laryngocele's definition carves its origin as distension of the laryngeal saccule (parameter 1), and the laryngeal ventricle's accepted definition carves the saccule as the blind pouch of the ventricle's anterior portion (parameters 2 and 3). Operational test (Law 8): remove the laryngeal ventricle now and the saccule with it - the mapped cystic distension has nothing to distend and the construct ceases to operate. Not identity (a distension of a pouch is not the pouch or the ventricle) and not purpose (Law 8c): the laryngocele is a clinical entity that needs the ventricle's saccule to exist.

payload.name: laryngeal-saccule
payload.scope: People made the laryngeal saccule construct to map the blind mucosal pouch of the laryngeal ventricle so that clinicians can diagnose laryngoceles and understand the route of lubricant delivery to the vocal fold mucosa.

definition.body: The laryngeal saccule is a human-authored anatomical construct mapping the blind mucosal pouch extending superiorly from the anterior portion of the laryngeal ventricle, whose mucous glands lubricate the vocal fold mucosa and which can become distended to form a laryngocele. Parameters: (1) the origin — the anterior recess of the laryngeal ventricle (ventriculus laryngis) between the vestibular and vocal folds; (2) the course — a vertical pouch extending upward between the vocalis muscle medially and the thyroid cartilage lamina laterally, reaching the level of the hyoid bone; (3) the contents — mucous glands secreting lubricant onto the superior surface of the vocal fold mucosa; (4) the clinical significance — distension produces an internal laryngocele (air-filled, communicating with the ventricle) or a mucocele (occluded, mucus-filled), and the saccule is the route for external extension through the thyrohyoid membrane. It persists as a standard anatomical landmark in laryngology, head and neck surgery, and airway management. e.g.: the laryngeal saccule as described in Cummings Otolaryngology, 6th edition; distended laryngeal saccule forming internal laryngocele on CT imaging; surgical excision of enlarged laryngeal saccule during laryngocelectomy | not: laryngeal ventricle (the hourglass recess whose anterior portion the saccule extends from); the laryngocele (the pathological distension of the saccule, not the normal saccule itself) [formal: sacculus laryngis | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

definition.body: The esophagus is a human-authored anatomical construct mapping the muscular conduit extending from the lower pharynx at the level of the cricoid cartilage (C6) to the stomach through the diaphragmatic hiatus (T10), whose primary function is transporting ingested material from the pharynx to the gastric lumen. Parameters: (1) the segments — cervical (C6 to thoracic inlet), thoracic (thoracic inlet to diaphragm), and abdominal (diaphragm to stomach); (2) the wall layers — mucosa (stratified squamous epithelium), submucosa with esophageal glands, muscularis externa (upper third skeletal muscle, middle third mixed, lower third smooth muscle), and adventitia; (3) the constrictions — four anatomical narrowings at the pharyngoesophageal junction, crossing of the aortic arch and left main bronchus, and esophageal hiatus, which are sites of foreign body impaction; (4) the clinical significance — gastroesophageal reflux disease, Barrett esophagus, esophageal varices, achalasia, and esophageal cancer staging. definition.body: The diaphragm is a human-authored anatomical construct mapping the dome-shaped skeletal muscle and central tendon that forms the floor of the thoracic cavity and the roof of the abdominal cavity, separating the two cavities and acting as the principal muscle of quiet inspiration. Parameters: (1) the three parts — the central tendon and the peripheral muscle belly formed by sternal, costal, and lumbar (crural) origins; (2) the crura — the right and left crura arising from the lumbar vertebrae that enclose the esophageal hiatus; (3) the apertures — the caval opening (T8, for the inferior vena cava), the esophageal hiatus (T10, for the esophagus and vagus), and the aortic hiatus (T12, for the aorta and thoracic duct); (4) the innervation and motion — the phrenic nerves (C3-C5) drive contraction, lowering the dome to expand the thorax on inspiration. It persists as a standard anatomical structure in human anatomy texts, thoracic and abdominal surgery, and respiratory physiology. e.g.: the diaphragm as described in Moore Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 9th edition; the right and left crura and esophageal hiatus shown on CT of a paraesophageal hernia; diaphragmatic dome excursion measured on a lateral chest radiograph | not: the pericardium (the fibrous sac enclosing the heart, a distinct structure); the pleura (the serous membrane lining the thoracic cavity and lungs, a distinct structure) [formal: diaphragma | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: phrenic-nerve

definition.body: The phrenic nerve is a human-authored anatomical construct mapping the paired mixed nerve arising from the cervical spinal nerves C3, C4, and C5 (the 'C3, 4, 5 keep the diaphragm alive' roots) that descends through the neck and thorax to the diaphragm, supplying it with motor fibers and carrying sensory fibers from the central diaphragm, pericardium, and mediastinal pleurae. Parameters: (1) the origin — ventral rami of C3, C4, and C5, joined in the neck behind the subclavian artery; (2) the course — descending on the anterior scalene in the neck, then through the mediastinum between the pericardium and mediastinal pleura, to the diaphragm; (3) the motor distribution — exclusive motor supply to the diaphragm (contraction lowers the dome on inspiration); (4) the sensory distribution — the central diaphragm, fibrous pericardium, and mediastinal pleurae, with irritation referred to the C3-C5 dermatome (shoulder-tip pain). It persists as a standard anatomical landmark in neuroanatomy texts, thoracic surgery, and respiratory physiology. e.g.: the phrenic nerve course shown in Gray's Anatomy; diaphragmatic paralysis from iatrogenic phrenic nerve injury during left thoracotomy; phrenic nerve stimulation measured during a fluoroscopic sniff test | not: the vagus nerve (CN X, a separate nerve descending in the tracheoesophageal groove); the accessory nerve (CN XI, which supplies the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius) [formal: nervus phrenicus | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: laryngeal-framework
payload.scope: Anatomists and airway surgeons needed a single stable name for the complete cartilaginous scaffold of the larynx, because laryngofissure, shunt surgery, and total laryngectomy are planned around the whole scaffold and its inter-cartilaginous joints, not around individual cartilages.

definition.body: The laryngeal framework is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the complete cartilaginous scaffold of the larynx — the thyroid, cricoid, and epiglottic cartilages with the paired arytenoid and corniculate cartilages, joined by the thyrohyoid, cricothyroid, cricotracheal, and thyroepiglottic ligaments and membranes — as one structural unit. Parameters: (1) composition — the six cartilages (thyroid, cricoid, epiglottis, two arytenoids, two corniculati) with the inter-cartilaginous ligaments and membranes that fix their relations; (2) function — the anchor for the intrinsic laryngeal muscles at the arytenoid muscular processes and the thyroid laminae, the suspension of the vocal folds, and the maintenance of the airway lumen against collapse; (3) clinical access — the framework is the operative field of laryngofissure, medialization thyroplasty, and total laryngectomy, and its articulations are the joints moved in arytenoid adduction and abduction. It persists as a standard anatomical structure in human anatomy texts, laryngology atlases, and airway surgery references. e.g.: the laryngeal framework diagrammed in the larynx chapter of Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition by Drake; the framework exposed during laryngofissure in an airway management procedure per Cummings Otolaryngology, 6th edition; the framework of a total laryngectomy specimen in an ENT surgery atlas | not: the thyroid cartilage alone (a single member of the framework, not the whole); the cricoid cartilage alone (a single member); the laryngeal inlet (the opening bounded by the framework, not the framework itself) [formal: armatura laryngis | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.reasoning: [3 test] The note's removal argument overstates the removal's consequence, so item 3 fails. The DEPENDS_ON test (Laws 8, 8a) asks: remove Y now, does X stop OPERATING? The note claims that removing the vagus nerve makes the esophagus 'cease to operate as a transport conduit.' That is not what the removal shows. Bilateral vagotomy leaves the esophagus in place, still structurally whole, still able to move material into the stomach by gravity and by the intrinsic myenteric plexus, which the note itself lists as part of the esophagus's own wall. What vagotomy actually produces is impaired motility, slower transit, and a non-relaxing lower esophageal sphincter (dysphagia and reflux) — a degraded, not stopped, conduit. An esophagus without its vagal supply still transports; it does not stop. The note's own premises (the myenteric plexus is innervated by vagal efferents; the LES 'cannot relax') show a partial failure of the removal test, which Law 8a says files no DEPENDS_ON edge. A true dependency is that the esophagus's parasympathetic regulation DEPENDS_ON the vagus, not that the esophagus itself cannot operate without it. STRIKE on [3 test].

payload.name: cricoarytenoid-joint
payload.scope: People made the cricoarytenoid joint construct to map the paired synovial articulation between the arytenoid cartilage and the cricoid cartilage that enables the rotation and sliding which abduct, adduct, and adjust the vocal folds, so that clinicians and voice scientists can understand laryngeal biomechanics relevant to phonation and laryngeal trauma.

definition.body: The cricoarytenoid joint is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the paired synovial joints where the base of each arytenoid cartilage articulates with the superior surface of the cricoid cartilage, whose rotation and sliding movements enable the vocal folds to be abducted, adducted, and adjusted in length and tension. Parameters: (1) the articulation — the cricoarytenoid facet on the base of the arytenoid cartilage against the corresponding facet on the superior surface of the cricoid cartilage; (2) the joint capsule — a thin fibrous capsule enclosing the articular surfaces; (3) the movements — rotation of the arytenoid on a vertical axis through the muscular process (abduction and adduction of the vocal folds) and sliding of the arytenoid base (approximation and lengthening); (4) the muscle action — the posterior cricoarytenoid abducts the fold by rotating the arytenoid, the lateral cricoarytenoid adducts it, and the thyroarytenoid contributes to approximation; (5) the functional outcome — the opening and closing of the glottis and the adjustment of vocal fold length and tension for phonation and airway protection. It persists as a standard anatomical landmark in human anatomy texts, laryngology classification systems, and surgical anatomy references. e.g.: the cricoarytenoid joint described in Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition by Drake; cricoarytenoid joint dislocation following blunt laryngeal trauma per Holinger's classification; the cricoarytenoid joint visualized on axial computed tomography of the larynx in airway evaluation | not: the cricothyroid joint (the articulation between the thyroid inferior horn and the cricoid cartilage); the arytenoid cartilage (the paired cartilage whose base forms one articular surface of the joint); the vocal process (the anterior projection of the arytenoid cartilage that anchors the vocal fold) [formal: articulatio cricoarytenoidea | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: trachealis-muscle
payload.scope: People made the trachealis-muscle construct to map the smooth muscle closing the posterior gap of the tracheal cartilages, so that clinicians can understand tracheal dynamics during respiration and manage airway obstruction.

definition.body: The trachealis muscle is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the smooth muscle band spanning the posterior open gap of the C-shaped tracheal cartilage rings, connecting adjacent cartilage ends and narrowing the tracheal lumen. Parameters: (1) the location — the posterior (membranous) wall of the trachea, between the free ends of successive C-shaped hyaline cartilage rings, running from the inferior border of the last tracheal ring to just above the carina; (2) the fiber orientation — longitudinal fibers running vertically, converging slightly toward the midline as they insert on the fibrous tissue between cartilage ends; (3) the innervation — autonomic innervation from the vagus nerve and sympathetic trunk, causing constriction of the tracheal lumen when activated; (4) the functional role — active narrowing of the tracheal lumen during forced expiration, coughing, and bronchoscopy, and passive contribution to the flexible posterior wall that allows esophageal distension during swallowing; (5) the clinical significance — target of botulinum toxin injection for airway disorders, landmark during tracheal resection surgery, and contributor to airway resistance in obstructive lung disease. It persists as a standard anatomical structure in human anatomy texts, pulmonology, and thoracic surgery references. e.g.: the trachealis muscle described in Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition by Drake; tracheal narrowing during coughing observed on high-resolution CT in Cummings Otolaryngology, 6th edition; the muscle targeted in tracheobronchomalacia management per ATS guidelines | not: the trachea (the entire cartilaginous airway tube, of which this is only one component); the bronchus (the airway below the tracheal bifurcation, distinct structure) [formal: musculus trachealis | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: tracheal-cartilage
payload.scope: People made the tracheal-cartilage construct to map the C-shaped hyaline rings that keep the tracheal lumen patent, so that clinicians can plan tracheostomy, resection, and airway reconstruction.

definition.body: The tracheal cartilage is a human-authored anatomical construct mapping the stacked C-shaped hyaline rings that form the cartilaginous framework of the trachea. Parameters: (1) number and shape — approximately 16-20 rings, each an incomplete C-shaped plate of hyaline cartilage, open posteriorly; (2) position — the rings stack from just below the cricoid cartilage to the level of the carina (T4-T5), separated by short intervals of fibrous membrane; (3) posterior completion — the open posterior gap of each ring is bridged by the trachealis muscle and the membranous posterior wall, which allows esophageal distension; (4) function — the rings keep the lumen patent against negative intrathoracic pressure while their incomplete shape preserves flexibility; (5) clinical role — landmarks for tracheostomy (typically the second to third rings), for tracheal resection and reconstruction, and the source of the calcified rings seen on chest radiographs. It persists as a standard anatomical structure in human anatomy texts, thoracic surgery references, and airway management protocols. e.g.: the tracheal cartilage rings described in the trachea chapter of Moore Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 9th edition; tracheostomy incision between the second and third tracheal rings per Cummings Otolaryngology, 6th edition; the tracheal rings calcified on a PA chest radiograph | not: the cricoid cartilage (the single complete ring above the trachea, a laryngeal cartilage); the trachealis muscle (the smooth muscle spanning the posterior gap, not cartilage); the bronchial cartilages (the irregular plates of the bronchi below the carina) [formal: cartilago trachealis | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: internal-laryngeal-nerve
payload.scope: People made the internal-laryngeal-nerve construct to map the sensory branch of the superior laryngeal nerve that pierces the thyrohyoid membrane, so that clinicians can perform targeted regional anesthesia and identify the nerve during thyroid and laryngeal surgery.

definition.body: The internal laryngeal nerve is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the sensory branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (CN X) which pierces the thyrohyoid membrane to provide visceral sensation to the laryngeal mucosa above the vocal folds. Parameters: (1) the origin — arises from the superior laryngeal nerve at the level of the inferior vagal ganglion, branching as the superior laryngeal nerve descends; (2) the course — travels anteroinferiorly alongside the superior laryngeal artery, piercing the thyrohyoid membrane between the thyroid cartilage and hyoid bone; (3) the sensory distribution — supplies general sensation to the laryngeal mucosa of the piriform fossa, the epiglottis, and the laryngeal surface of the vallecula, all above the vocal folds; (4) the reflex function — carries the afferent limb of the cough reflex when the mucosa above the vocal folds is stimulated. It persists as a standard anatomical landmark in head and neck surgery texts, regional anesthesia atlases, and laryngology references. e.g.: the internal laryngeal nerve course described in Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition by Drake; internal laryngeal nerve block for laryngoscopy anesthesia per Cummings Otolaryngology, 6th edition; sensory testing of the internal laryngeal nerve using cotton swab stimulation above the vocal folds | not: the superior-laryngeal-nerve (the parent trunk before it divides); the external-laryngeal-nerve (the motor branch, not the sensory branch) [formal: nervus laryngeus superior internus | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: external-laryngeal-nerve
payload.scope: People made the external-laryngeal-nerve construct to map the motor branch of the superior laryngeal nerve that innervates the cricothyroid muscle, so that surgeons can preserve it during thyroidectomy and neck dissection.

definition.body: The external laryngeal nerve is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the motor branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (CN X) which descends on the inferior pharyngeal constrictor to innervate the cricothyroid muscle. Parameters: (1) the origin — arises from the superior laryngeal nerve as it branches from the inferior vagal ganglion; (2) the course — descends on the inferior pharyngeal constrictor muscle alongside the superior laryngeal artery, passing deep to the inferior constrictor; (3) the motor distribution — supplies motor innervation exclusively to the cricothyroid muscle, with minor branches to the inferior pharyngeal constrictor; (4) the functional outcome — the cricothyroid muscle, innervated by the external laryngeal nerve, tilts the thyroid cartilage forward to increase tension on the vocal folds and raise pitch. It persists as a standard anatomical landmark in head and neck surgery texts, laryngology references, and regional anesthesia protocols. e.g.: the external laryngeal nerve course described in Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition by Drake; external laryngeal nerve identification during total thyroidectomy per Cummings Otolaryngology, 6th edition; external laryngeal nerve injury causing voice fatigue after thyroidectomy per Cummings Otolaryngology, 6th edition | not: the superior-laryngeal-nerve (the parent trunk before it divides); the internal-laryngeal-nerve (the sensory branch, not the motor branch) [formal: nervus laryngeus superior externus | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]
